name: Zara Emberveil
equipment: Book of Shadows (Pact of the Tome — a journal bound in deep blue leather with silver wave patterns)
A scroll case with fragments of Sallith's last prophecy
A blanket of woven sea-grass (gift from patron)
A vial of salt water that never evaporates
A small mirror with a cracked frame
features: Hellish Resistance (Tiefling racial — resistance to fire damage)

Infernal Legacy (Tiefling racial — you know the Thaumaturgy cantrip; at 3rd level, you can cast Hellish Rebuke as a 2nd-level spell once per long rest; at 5th level, you can cast Darkness once per long rest; CHA is the spellcasting ability for these)
Otherworldly Patron: The Celestial (Sallith — the murdered wife of storm giant King Vethran, now a disgraced empyrean spirit seeking vengeance through a mortal vessel)
Pact Boon: Pact of the Tome (your Book of Shadows contains 3 cantrips from any class list; you can also inscribe rituals from any class via Book of Ancient Secrets)
Eldritch Invocations: Agonizing Blast (add your CHA modifier to each beam of Eldritch Blast damage; +4 per beam)

Eldritch Invocations: Book of Ancient Secrets (you can inscribe magical rituals from any class into your Book of Shadows; you have Detect Magic and Comprehend Languages as rituals; you can inscribe other found rituals for 50gp and 2 hours each)

Healing Light (Celestial Warlock — you have a pool of d6s equal to 1 + your warlock level = 6d6; as a bonus action, you can heal one creature you can see within 60 feet by spending dice from the pool, up to your CHA modifier = 4 dice at once; pool replenishes on long rest)
Pact Magic (2 spell slots that recharge on short or long rest, cast at 3rd level)

Discovery (Hermit feature — the quiet seclusion of your hermitage gave you access to a unique and powerful discovery; Zara's discovery is fragments of Sallith's final prophecy, which contain insider knowledge about the conspiracy against King Vethran)

personality.traits: I deflect sincerity with sarcasm — the more important something is to me, the more flippant I sound talking about it. I have a habit of referring to my patron by increasingly casual nicknames ('Sallith,' 'the Queen,' 'my dead boss,' 'the angrier half of my brain') that would be deeply disrespectful if Sallith did not seem to find them amusing. I sleep badly and talk in my sleep, always in Giant, which I do not consciously speak fluently.
personality.ideals: Power is a transaction, and honesty about the terms is the only real virtue. Sallith gave me power in exchange for vengeance, and I accepted with open eyes. I do not pretend to be a hero — I am a weapon pointed at the people who murdered my patron. If that happens to save the world, wonderful. If not, at least I was honest about my motives.
personality.bonds: Sallith chose me — a tiefling hermit with no connections, no reputation, and no reason to say no — because she needed someone expendable and angry. I accepted because I was both. But something has changed. The visions Sallith sends me are not just tactical briefings; they are memories. I have seen Vethran through her eyes. I have felt her love for her daughters. I am no longer just a weapon. I am carrying a dead woman's heart, and I do not know how to put it down.
personality.flaws: I keep secrets reflexively, even from allies. Sallith has given me fragments of insider knowledge about the conspiracy against Vethran — names, locations, motives — and I parcel them out strategically rather than sharing everything. I tell myself this is tactical caution, but the truth is that information is the only currency I have ever had, and I cannot bring myself to spend it all at once. This makes me a difficult party member to trust.

appearance: Zara Emberveil is the kind of person who walks into a room and makes everyone slightly uncomfortable without doing anything obviously wrong. She is tall for a woman — five feet ten inches — with the lean, angular build of someone who forgets to eat when she is thinking. Her skin is a deep wine-red, the color of old burgundy, smooth and unmarked except for a pattern of faintly luminous silver lines that trace across her left forearm and hand like veins of moonlight — the mark of her celestial pact, which appeared the night Sallith claimed her. Her horns curve backward from her temples in elegant arcs, dark as obsidian, and she has filed the tips to dull points — not for aesthetics but because she kept catching them on doorframes. Her eyes are solid gold, without pupil or iris, and they glow faintly in darkness with a warm light that contradicts the sharp, sardonic expression they usually carry. Her hair is ink-black, long and straight, worn loose most of the time and tucked behind her horns. A thin, prehensile tail — dark red, tipped in a small spade shape — extends from the base of her spine and has a mind of its own, curling and uncurling with her mood like a cat's. She wears studded leather armor under a long, deep-blue coat that she claims was a gift from her patron but which looks suspiciously like it was stolen from a naval officer. Her Book of Shadows — a journal bound in blue leather with silver wave patterns — hangs from a chain at her belt. The most unsettling detail is her shadow, which does not always match her movements: sometimes it gestures when she is still, or turns its head to look at things Zara is not looking at, as though someone else is wearing it.
backstory:
Zara Emberveil spent most of her life trying to disappear. Being a tiefling in the Cormorant Coast was not inherently dangerous — the region was more tolerant than most — but it was exhausting. The stares, the whispered prayers, the mothers who pulled their children closer when she walked past. Zara learned early that the easiest way to deal with people's fear was to not deal with people at all.

She left civilization at nineteen, retreating to a sea cave on the coast north of Anchorhold, where the cliffs were too steep for casual visitors and the tides were too treacherous for anyone else. She became a hermit in the truest sense — no visitors, no correspondence, no contact with the outside world for nearly five years. She studied the tides, collected herbs, taught herself the languages of old texts she found washed up in sealed jars (Abyssal, Giant, fragments of Primordial), and cultivated a comfortable misanthropy that she wore like armor.

She was twenty-four when Sallith found her.

The storm came from nowhere — a supernatural tempest that battered the coast for three days, driving waves into Zara's cave and forcing her to cling to the highest ledge to avoid drowning. On the third night, as the water rose to her chin, a light appeared in the depths. Not the cold light of deep-sea creatures, but something warm and golden, like sunlight filtered through water. Zara, half-drowned and hallucinating, reached for it.

The light was Sallith. Or what remained of Sallith.

Sallith had been the wife of King Vethran, ruler of the storm giants — the highest of all giant-kind under the Vaunting. She had been an empyrean, a being of near-divine power, beloved by her husband and her three daughters. And she had been murdered. Assassinated by agents of a conspiracy that Zara did not yet understand, a plot to destabilize the Vaunting and plunge the giant races into chaos. Sallith's death had been the first move in a longer game, and it had worked: Vethran, mad with grief, had vanished. The Vaunting had shattered. And the giants, leaderless and purposeless, were tearing the world apart.

Sallith's spirit should have passed on. Empyreans do not linger. But her rage — her fury at being murdered, her terror for her daughters, her desperate need to see justice done — had anchored her to the mortal plane as a disembodied consciousness, too weak to act but too angry to rest. She needed a vessel. She needed hands, and eyes, and a voice. She needed someone with nothing to lose and enough bitterness to say yes.

She found Zara.

The pact was simple, as all the best pacts are. Sallith would give Zara power — celestial power, the healing light and sacred flame of an empyrean's grace, channeled through a mortal frame. In exchange, Zara would be Sallith's agent in the world. She would find the conspirators who had murdered Sallith. She would expose them. And she would make them pay.

Zara said yes before Sallith finished the offer. She told herself it was because the power was too good to refuse, and that was partly true. But there was another reason, one she does not admit: she recognized something in Sallith's rage. The fury of someone who had been discarded, dismissed, destroyed by forces larger than herself. Zara knew that feeling. She had lived with it her entire life.

Since the pact, Zara has learned more than she expected. Sallith sends her visions — fragments of memory, glimpses of the conspiracy, names and faces that surface in dreams. Zara knows things she should not know: that Vethran is alive but imprisoned. That his daughter Vesarra is trying to hold the storm giant court together. That the conspiracy reaches beyond the giants, involving entities that profit from chaos. She parcels this knowledge out carefully, never revealing everything, because information is leverage and Zara has spent her whole life with very little of it.

She has also begun to feel things she did not expect. Sallith's memories are not just tactical — they are personal. Zara has seen Vethran through Sallith's eyes, felt the warmth of a love that spanned centuries. She has watched Sallith's daughters grow up in borrowed memories, felt a mother's pride and fear. She went into this pact as a weapon, but she is becoming something else — a witness, a mourner, a carrier of grief that is not her own but has become inseparable from her heart. She does not know what to do with that.
